name: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
description: This work systematically studies object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It evaluates several representative LVLMs on MSCOCO using CHAIR and proposes a polling-based query method called POPE for more stable and flexible evaluation of object hallucination. The paper also analyzes how visual instruction data distributions influence hallucination and extends evaluation with automatic segmentation tools such as SEEM.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
rai:dataCollection: The evaluation data are built from existing image datasets. For CHAIR evaluation, the authors randomly sample 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions from the validation set of MSCOCO. For POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in the annotations and construct 6 questions for each image. POPE constructs triples consisting of an image, multiple object-probing questions, and Yes/No answers. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation results using SEEM. Negative objects are sampled under Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data come from existing datasets including MSCOCO validation images with object annotations and human-labeled captions, and additionally A-OKVQA and GQA images for SEEM-based POPE. Objects used for probing are sourced either from human annotations or from automatic segmentation outputs generated by SEEM.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For POPE, the authors convert object hallucination evaluation into a binary classification setup by constructing triples of image, object-probing question, and Yes/No answer. They set the ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects as 1:1 for label balance. Nonexistent objects are selected using three sampling strategies: Random Sampling from objects not in the image, Popular Sampling from the top-k most frequent objects in the dataset not in the current image, and Adversarial Sampling from top-k co-occurring objects with ground-truth objects that do not exist in the image.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For CHAIR on MSCOCO, the authors follow Rohrbach et al. (2018) and only consider the 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge. They prompt LVLMs to generate captions for sampled MSCOCO images and compute CHAIR on these captions. For POPE on MSCOCO, they randomly select 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects and construct 6 questions per image. For unannotated settings, they use SEEM to annotate images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA before building POPE.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The study uses existing human annotations from MSCOCO for contained objects and human-labeled captions. In POPE, labels are formulated as Yes/No answers to object-probing questions based on whether the probed object is a ground-truth object in the image or a sampled nonexistent object. For scalability experiments, images are automatically annotated with SEEM to obtain objects for question construction. For VQA evaluation, ChatGPT is used to judge whether a model's open-ended answer matches one of the candidate correct answers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes stability by comparing POPE and CHAIR under different prompt templates and reports that POPE has lower standard deviation. It also analyzes consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and generated captions: for InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4, objects receiving No responses were rarely mentioned in captions, while most objects mentioned in captions received Yes responses. The paper also notes divergence between annotation-based and SEEM-based POPE due to finer granularity and possible inconsistency between SEEM labels and human annotations.
rai:annotationsPerItem: For POPE on MSCOCO, 6 questions per image are constructed.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that hallucination hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment and may result in unexpected consequences caused by hallucinated objects. It gives autonomous driving as an example, where incorrect understanding of the external environment could lead to wrong decisions and serious safety issues. The authors hope the work can help develop more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs.
rai:dataBiases: The paper empirically reveals that object distributions in visual instruction datasets affect hallucination. LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects in the visual instruction datasets and objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image. It also notes that synthetic visual instructions generated by unimodal LLMs may involve unexpected descriptive information inconsistent with the image, which could mislead LVLMs.
rai:dataLimitations: The work only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM capability. Due to computational limitations, all models are evaluated on only part of each dataset validation set, so results may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine whether models answer Yes or No, and models may fail to provide explicit Yes/No words, causing inaccurate evaluation. When combined with automatic segmentation, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to divergence in results. The study also compares only a small number of LVLMs and excludes some recently released or closed-source models.
rai:dataUseCases: The datasets are used for evaluation of object hallucination in LVLMs. MSCOCO is used for CHAIR and POPE evaluation, while A-OKVQA and GQA are used for SEEM-based POPE and VQA comparison. POPE is designed as a stable, fair, and flexible evaluation approach and can be extended to unannotated datasets with automatic segmentation tools.
